slides.title: Lvalues and Rvalues Fundamentals
slides.prompt: Every expression in C++ has a type and a value category. An lvalue refers to a memory location with a persistent identity (has a name and addressable memory). An rvalue represents temporary data with no persistent identity.
slides.codeSnippet:
int x = 10; // 'x' is an lvalue, '10' is an rvalue
int y = x + 5; // 'x + 5' produces a temporary rvalue

slides.title: Addressable Memory Identifiers
slides.prompt: Fill in the operator that can be applied to lvalues to retrieve their memory address, but fails on rvalues.
slides.codeSnippet:
int a = 42;
int* ptr = ___a; // Valid because 'a' is an lvalue

slides.title: Value Category of String Literals
slides.prompt: What value category does a string literal like "Hello, World!" belong to in C++?
options: Lvalue expression (it resides in static memory and has an addressable location)
Prvalue expression (it is purely temporary without memory)
Xvalue expression (an expiring value ready for move)
slides.correctAnswer: Lvalue expression (it resides in static memory and has an addressable location)

slides.title: Prvalues and Temporary Objects
slides.prompt: Fill in the standard term for a pure rvalue that initializes an object or computes a value.
slides.codeSnippet:
// '5 + 3' is a pure rvalue, also known as a ___value
int val = 5 + 3;

slides.title: Primary Taxonomies of C++11 Value Categories
slides.prompt: Which expression category encompasses both prvalues (pure rvalues) and xvalues (eXpiring values)?

slides.title: Xvalue (eXpiring Value)
slides.prompt: Fill in the cast operator that turns an lvalue into an expiring value (xvalue).
slides.codeSnippet:
std::string name = "C++";
std::string target = std::___(name); // 'name' becomes an xvalue

slides.title: Modifying Rvalues
slides.prompt: Which statement regarding class-type rvalues is correct?
options: Member functions can be invoked on class-type rvalues, and they can be modified unless marked with lvalue ref-qualifiers
Rvalues can never have member methods called on them
Rvalues automatically convert to non-const lvalue references
Built-in primitive rvalues (like int) allow direct assignment
slides.correctAnswer: Member functions can be invoked on class-type rvalues, and they can be modified unless marked with lvalue ref-qualifiers

slides.title: Const Lvalue References
slides.prompt: Fill in the reference type that can bind to temporary rvalues without allowing modifications.
slides.codeSnippet: ___ std::string& ref = std::string("Temp"); // Extends temporary lifetime

slides.title: Lifetime Extension of Temporaries
slides.prompt: What happens when a temporary object is bound to a const lvalue reference?
options: The lifetime of the temporary object is extended to match the scope of the reference
A deep copy is created immediately on the stack
The temporary is destroyed at the end of the full expression statement
A compilation error occurs unless std::move is used
slides.correctAnswer: The lifetime of the temporary object is extended to match the scope of the reference
